nodes.name: GtfsShapeRepository.java
nodes.summary: Spring repository that lazily builds each STPT line's drawable paths from the GTFS zip, using shapes.txt per distinct shape_id and falling back to ordered stop sequences for trips without a shape, with simplified, de-duplicated paths.

nodes.name: GtfsShapeRepository

nodes.name: parse

nodes.name: stopSequencePaths
nodes.summary: Builds fallback paths for shapeless trips by joining their ordered stop positions from stops.txt and stop_times.txt, grouped by route in sorted trip order.

nodes.name: addPath
nodes.summary: Adds a path to a set after removing consecutive duplicate points, dropping paths with fewer than two points.

nodes.name: each

tour.title: Project Vision and Plan
tour.description: Start here: the README is only a title, so the real orientation comes from AGENTS.md and PLAN.md. AGENTS.md states the hackathon challenge (Connected Communities), the core feature list for Timisoara (filterable places map, live STPT transit and last-tram info, directions, events with QR check-in and reliability points, profiles, an AI assistant) and the team rules for package structure, tests and docs. PLAN.md breaks this into numbered tasks, which is why many files reference PLAN section numbers.

tour.title: Living Docs and the API Contract
tour.description: DOCS.md is the living documentation hub: architecture, configuration, the Supabase database, external data sources (STPT, LiveTickets, OpenStreetMap, Gemini) and the reliability rules. docs/API.md is the contract between the Spring backend and the mobile app, defining shared conventions for paged and error answers and every endpoint. Keep both open as a reference; every later step implements part of them.

tour.title: Profiles and Events Schema
tour.description: The data model starts in Supabase migrations. Profiles extend Supabase Auth users with a username and reliability score, and events store user-created or imported happenings with a location, time and optional capacity. These two tables are the backbone of the social side of the app.

tour.title: Participation and Reliability Schema
tour.description: Building on profiles and events, event_participants records who joined which event (and their QR token), while reliability_log keeps an auditable history of points gained for attending or lost for no-shows. schema_checks.sql is a self-rolling-back test block that verifies these database rules, such as profile creation on sign-up.

tour.title: Places and Researched Menu Prices
tour.description: The places table holds OpenStreetMap points of interest for the map. The newer place_prices table stores researched menu prices (COFFEE, PIZZA, FOOD, BEER, DRINK) in lei with their source, matched to places by name or brand so chain prices apply to every branch. The seed migrations fill it with real Timisoara prices, which is what lets the AI answer how much a coffee will cost.

tour.title: Spring Boot Entry, Settings and Build
tour.description: BackendApplication is the Spring Boot entry point (Java 21, Spring Boot 4). application.properties configures Hibernate schema validation against the Supabase migrations and the connection pool, SupabaseProperties binds the Supabase settings, and build.gradle declares JPA, Security, Validation and Web MVC. Run the backend tests with ./gradlew test in backend/.

tour.title: Security and the Current User
tour.description: SecurityConfig validates Supabase-issued JWTs so the backend never handles passwords. CurrentUser extracts the authenticated user id for controllers, and the JSON entry point and access-denied handler make 401 and 403 answers use the same error format as the rest of the API.

tour.title: One Error Format and Paging
tour.description: ErrorCode and ApiException are among the most depended-on files in the backend: services throw ApiException with a code, and GlobalExceptionHandler turns it into the shared error body from docs/API.md. PageParams and PageResponse give every list endpoint the same paging shape.

tour.title: Backend Tests with Real JWTs
tour.description: Tests sign real JWTs with JwtTestTokens so security runs exactly as in production, and the test profile swaps Supabase for an in-memory H2 database in PostgreSQL mode. SecurityConfigTest and GlobalExceptionHandlerTest pin down the cross-cutting behaviour from the previous two steps.

tour.title: Users and Profiles Feature
tour.description: The users package shows the project's standard layering: controller, service interface with impl, repository, domain entity and mapper. UserController serves profile lookup, search and username edits, while the attended-events repository feeds the public profile history.

tour.title: Places: From OpenStreetMap to the Map
tour.description: PlaceImportServiceImpl pulls points of interest from the Overpass API and maps OSM tags to PlaceCategory, the categories that drive the map filter chips. PlaceController answers bbox, category and distance queries using the shared GeoPoint type, one of the most widely used files in the backend.

tour.title: Opening Hours and Stored Prices
tour.description: These files enrich places for the AI assistant. OpeningHours parses common OSM opening_hours formats to answer whether a place is open at a given local time, and PlacePrice with PlacePriceRepository reads the researched menu prices from Step 5 by lower-cased place name. PlaceService exposes an explore query that returns places together with their prices.

tour.title: Live Transit: Caching and the STPT Client
tour.description: Live STPT data is fetched over HTTP by StptClientImpl, configured by StptProperties. StaleCache keeps the last good answer so the app keeps working when STPT is slow or down, and its test uses a MutableClock to control time deterministically; the client test replays saved STPT answers.

tour.title: Live Transit: Service, Timetable and Endpoints
tour.description: TransitServiceImpl combines live STPT arrivals and vehicles with the GTFS timetable to answer nearby summaries, stop arrivals and the last departure of the day per line (the last tram feature). TransitMapperImpl converts raw STPT records into API DTOs and TransitController exposes them.

tour.title: Transit Line Shapes from GTFS
tour.description: To draw the whole tram, trolleybus and bus network, the backend reads every line's path from the STPT GTFS zip. GtfsShapeRepository builds these paths from shapes.txt, falls back to ordered stop_times sequences when a line has no shape, de-duplicates them and loads them lazily once behind the ShapeRepository interface. Each RouteShape is sent as a TransitShapeDto whose paths are Google encoded polylines produced by PolylineEncoder, matching the decoder the app already uses for directions. Before encoding, PathSimplifier thins each path with Douglas-Peucker at a 5 m tolerance, cutting the network from 41,729 to 9,668 points so the map stays smooth without visibly changing the lines.
tour.languageLesson: Google's encoded polyline format stores coordinate deltas at 5-decimal precision as compact ASCII characters, so a long path travels as a short string instead of a large JSON array of points.

tour.title: Directions with OpenTripPlanner
tour.description: Directions come from a self-hosted OpenTripPlanner 2 server. RoutingServiceImpl asks OtpGraphQlClient for walking or walking plus transit itineraries and returns legs with encoded polylines. The docker-compose file and the OTP README describe how to download the STPT GTFS and OSM data and run the server.

tour.title: Events and Participation API
tour.description: Events are the social core. EventController and EventServiceImpl handle listing, creating, joining and leaving events, enforcing capacity, while the repositories persist events and participants in the tables from Steps 3 and 4. The integration test checks these rules against a real database schema.

tour.title: QR Check-in, Reliability Points and Event Reviews
tour.description: At the event the organiser scans a participant's QR code; CheckInServiceImpl validates the token and awards reliability points. NoShowJob runs on a schedule and NoShowServiceImpl deducts points from participants who never checked in, writing to the reliability_log from Step 4. After a scan, the checked-in attendee can rate the event 1-5 stars with a short comment (reviews package: ReviewController, ReviewServiceImpl); 24 hours after the event ends ReviewSettlementJob turns the average into -5..+5 reliability points for the organiser, logged as EVENT_RATING.

tour.title: Importing Parties and Concerts
tour.description: Besides user-created events, the map shows events imported from LiveTickets. EventImportServiceImpl fetches them, LiveTicketsEventMapperImpl converts them into events, and VenueGeocoderImpl places them on the map, using venues.txt for venues OpenStreetMap misses.

tour.title: AI Assistant: Endpoint and Contract
tour.description: The AI assistant answers questions such as where to drink cheap coffee nearby and what it will cost. AiController exposes authenticated POST /ai/chat; ChatRequest carries the full stateless conversation plus an optional location, and ChatResponse returns the reply text with place and event cards and price sources. InMemoryChatRateLimiter throttles each user with a one-minute sliding window, and AiProperties holds limits such as tool rounds and conversation length.

tour.title: AI Chat Service: The Tool Loop
tour.description: AiChatServiceImpl is the heart of the assistant. It converts the conversation into Gemini turns, adds the SystemPrompt (current Timisoara time, location status, and the rule to quote only stored data), then runs a bounded loop: the model asks for tools, the tools run in parallel, and their results go back to the model until it writes a final answer. ToolContext is shared per request and collects the places, events and planned routes the tools returned, and decides whether a route starts from the user.

tour.title: AI Tools over Our Own Data
tour.description: Each tool wraps a service from earlier steps so the model answers from the app's data instead of guessing. search_places uses the places, opening hours and stored prices from Steps 11-12 and is the only price source; search_events uses the events service; transit_info answers last-tram and next-arrival questions; plan_route uses OpenTripPlanner routing with a walking fallback.

tour.title: The Gemini Client
tour.description: GeminiClient abstracts one generateContent call so the chat service can be tested with a fake. GeminiRestClient sends the API key header, classifies 429, 5xx and timeouts as retryable and reads retry-delay hints, which the service uses to fall back across the ordered free-tier models in GeminiProperties. GeminiPart models text, function calls and function responses in the wire format.

tour.title: Turning Replies into Cards
tour.description: After the loop ends, ChatResultMapperImpl builds the ChatResponse. It strips bold markdown, matches bold or whole-word names in the reply to the places and events collected in ToolContext (in reply order), and attaches up to five price source pages as SourceDto. It also turns routes from plan_route into deduplicated ChatRouteDto cards whose RoutePointDto ends carry display names and a startsFromUser flag. This is how a plain-text answer becomes tappable cards in the app.

tour.title: Testing the AI Assistant
tour.description: The AI tests never call the real Gemini API. AiChatServiceImplTest drives the tool loop, forced last round, model fallback and quota retry with a fake client; GeminiRestClientTest uses a local HTTP server; tool tests mock the underlying services; and the controller and mapper tests pin down the API shape and card matching.

tour.title: Expo App Setup, Router and Auth
tour.description: The frontend is an Expo SDK 54 app using Expo Router, configured by package.json and app.json (deep linking, camera and location permissions). The root _layout wraps providers and an auth gate so signed-out users only reach the auth screens, AuthProvider holds the Supabase session, and client.ts is the single API client that attaches the access token and maps failures to typed errors.

tour.title: Blue/Gold Design System
tour.description: Before reading the screens, meet the visual language they share. theme.ts holds the design tokens (colours, spacing, radii, type scale) for the "Timisoara after dark" palette: night-navy surfaces with gold accents, and it is the most depended-on file in the whole graph. RoutePlate is a yellow transit-signage route-number plate in three sizes, reused for line numbers and the reliability score, and docs/design/mockups.html shows every screen in this palette as static HTML/CSS mockups.

tour.title: Tabs and the Home Screen
tour.description: The tab layout defines four bottom tabs: Home, Map, AI and Profile. The Home screen shows a search field, category chips, nearby upcoming events and the city info strip, which is now a departure board: the last-tram message, the last departure time in large gold numerals and an expandable transit alerts pill, styled with the tokens and route plates from the previous step. The events list adds search and filters. The CityInfoStrip on Home now also shows a next-arrival strip for the nearest stop, fed by the backend NextArrivalDto (line, destination and minutes until the next vehicle).

tour.title: The Map Tab: Places and Events
tour.description: map.tsx combines react-native-maps with place and event markers, filter chips, the transit layer, directions and a bottom panel, and can switch into journey mode when opened from an AI route card. MapContext is the shared state contract: a debounced visible bounding box, the user position, a single panel selection and the directions destination. Markers cluster when zoomed out and load data for the visible area through hooks such as usePlaces.

tour.title: Map Filters and the Live Network
tour.description: The Map tab's filter row (All places, categories, Events, Transport) is driven by mapFilters, a pure reducer that guarantees at least one layer always stays visible. With Transport on, TransitLayer draws every line shape from the previous backend step in its colour along with live vehicles and visible stops, highlighting a chosen line. VehicleMarker renders each vehicle as a memoised line-coloured badge so the 10-second position updates stay cheap, VehiclePanel shows speed and report age for a selected vehicle, and lines.ts holds the shared pure helpers such as deterministic line colours and vehicle icons. While directions are shown the map enters a focus mode: the filters are switched off and greyed out so only the user, the route, its live vehicles and the destination remain. Performance work keeps panning fluid: markers and ShapeLines are memoised, only vehicles inside the visible region are rendered, and all markers share a single refresh timer instead of one each.
tour.languageLesson: A reducer is a pure function (state, action) => newState. Keeping filter logic in one reducer makes rules like 'never hide every layer' easy to unit test without rendering the map.

tour.title: Stops, Ride Legs and Transit Hooks
tour.description: Beyond the network layer, StopPanel opens when a stop is tapped and lists the next live or timetable arrivals plus each line's last departure today. LegVehicles shows the live vehicles of the lines a route plan rides, so directions and journey mode show them even when the Transport filter is off. useTransit wraps the transit endpoints from Steps 14 and 15 in TanStack Query hooks, refreshing live vehicles every 10 seconds.

tour.title: Directions on the Map
tour.description: Tapping Directions on a place or event sets a destination in MapContext. DirectionsPanel compares walking and walking plus public transport times and shows per-leg steps, DirectionsLayer decodes and draws the route polylines (dashed for walking, solid for rides), and useRouting calls the OpenTripPlanner-backed endpoint from Step 16. tripSteps.ts turns an itinerary into ordered trip guidance (where to board, where to get off, where to walk), and TripMarkers.tsx draws those board / get off / walk markers on the map in each line's colour.

tour.title: The AI Chat Screen
tour.description: The AI tab is the frontend for Steps 20-24. useAi keeps the message history, trims it to the maximum window and sends it with the user location through endpoints.ai. ChatBubble shows replies with cited price sources, and ResultCards renders the place and event cards with a Show on map shortcut that deep-links into the Map tab; route answers get their own cards, covered next. Home AI shortcuts let users save a favourite question (SaveShortcut), keep it in shortcuts.ts storage, and fire it from the ShortcutBar on Home straight into this chat.

tour.title: AI Navigation and Journey Mode
tour.description: Building on the route cards from Step 24, RouteCards shows each AI-planned walk or walk + transit route with its duration and distance, a Show route on map preview and a Go button that checks location permission. navigation.ts encodes the route into Map tab params and parses it back into a validated request, so the Map tab from Step 29 opens in journey mode. There useJourney watches GPS, re-plans from the live position when the user goes off-route and detects arrival, using the pure maths in progress.ts, while JourneyPanel draws the legs and the current step with time and distance left.

tour.title: Events, Tickets and Profiles
tour.description: The event details screen lets users join or leave and shows participants with their reliability. The ticket screen displays the participant's QR code (holding only the qrToken) and the organiser's scanner checks people in, awarding the points from Step 18. Public profiles show attended events and the reliability score drawn by ReliabilityLine as a 0-200 transit line with stops every 50 points and a yellow route plate marking the score, followed by the scoring rules as a fare table. The event page also shows live reviews (stars, reviewer, comment) and a rating form for checked-in attendees.

tour.title: Frontend Verification
tour.description: Frontend tests use Jest and React Native Testing Library against mock backend routes, so screens are tested without a server. The map tests cover the filter reducer and chip colours, the live transit network, vehicle markers and panel, directions and journey flows, and the AI chat test covers sending, thinking, sources, errors and rate limits.
